title: Rice Spirits Explained
description: Rice spirits are among the world's oldest alcoholic drinks, deeply rooted in Asian culture. Learn how Baijiu, Shochu and Rice Whisky are made, where they come from and how they're evolving in modern bars and restaurants. Written for bartenders, retailers and curious drinkers.
topics: How rice spirits are made and where they come from
Rice spirits in modern bars and restaurants

lessons.title: Welcome to Rice Spirits Explained
lessons.review:
Rice spirits are distilled across Asia: Chinese baijiu and shaojiu, Japanese shochu, Okinawan awamori, Korean soju, and now rice whisky.

Baijiu, China's national spirit, is the most consumed spirit in the world by volume, though much of it is made from sorghum rather than rice.

This course covers their history, how they are made, the main styles, and how bartenders are mixing them today.

questions.q: Which spirit is China's national spirit?

lessons.title: A history of rice spirits
lessons.review:
Rice has been fermented in China for thousands of years. Distillation became widespread there later, and distilled rice spirits spread through East and Southeast Asia along trade routes.

Okinawa's awamori is believed to trace back to distilling techniques that arrived through trade with Siam (Thailand) in the 1400s, and it is still made with long-grain Thai rice.

Each culture shaped its own style, from Japan's single-distilled honkaku shochu to China's powerful, aromatic baijiu.

questions.q: Awamori's techniques are believed to have come through trade with?
questions.explain: Trade with Siam brought distilling to Okinawa.
It goes back thousands of years.

lessons.title: Types and styles of rice spirits
lessons.review:
Baijiu is grouped by aroma: strong aroma, light aroma, sauce aroma (the style of Moutai) and rice aroma, which is light, floral and clean.

Japanese kome shochu is made from rice and usually distilled once, keeping the character of its raw ingredient. Soju is Korea's everyday spirit.

New-wave producers are ageing rice spirits in oak to create rice whisky.

questions.explain: Rice aroma is the lightest style.

questions.q: Moutai is an example of which aroma?

lessons.title: How baijiu is made
lessons.review:
Baijiu uses qu, a starter of moulds and yeasts grown on grain, which breaks down starch and ferments it at the same time.

Much baijiu is fermented in solid state: damp grain packed into pits or jars rather than a liquid mash.

It is then distilled, often steamed through the fermented grain, aged in clay jars, and blended to a house style.

options: A starter of moulds and yeasts
questions.explain: Qu converts starch and ferments at once.

options: In solid state, in pits or jars

lessons.title: Turning baijiu into rice whisky
lessons.review:
Rice whisky takes a clean, rice-based spirit and matures it in oak casks, the way whisky makers mature malt.

The oak adds colour, vanilla and spice while the rice keeps a light, floral base.

Brands such as Grand Talon are introducing whisky drinkers to rice spirits through familiar serves like the highball.

questions.q: What turns a rice spirit into rice whisky?

questions.explain: Oak brings colour and sweet spice.
The highball is a great entry point.

lessons.title: The future of rice spirits
lessons.review:
Bartenders worldwide are discovering rice spirits for their clean, aromatic profiles.

Lighter styles, lower-ABV bottlings and cocktail-friendly releases are helping them reach new drinkers outside Asia.

For venues, rice spirits are a point of difference on the back bar and a story to tell guests.

options: A point of difference and a story

lessons.title: Mixing it: the rice whisky highball
lessons.review:
The highball is the easiest way to introduce rice whisky: a tall glass packed with ice, a measure of spirit and chilled soda water.

Stir gently to keep the bubbles. A twist of citrus peel lifts the floral notes.

Other easy serves include baijiu and tonic, a Negroni twist with shaojiu and rice wine, and a baijiu Margarita.

options: Spirit, lots of ice and chilled soda
